oil.summary: Crude cratered today as a US-Iran preliminary peace deal and agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz blindsided the market. WTI shed 4.06% to $81.43/bbl and Brent fell 4.23% to $83.64, extending brutal month-to-date losses of roughly 20% on both benchmarks. RBOB gasoline dropped 4.85% while heating oil led the complex lower at -5.50%. The Hormuz reopening removes a significant geopolitical risk premium that had been supporting prices, with options markets now pricing a 77% probability of an OPEC cut at the next meeting, suggesting the cartel faces renewed pressure. Cross-currents remain: Ukraine drone strikes hit a Russian oil facility on June 14, Britain intercepted a Russian shadow-fleet tanker in the English Channel, and the EU announced fresh sanctions targeting Russian energy revenues — but none were sufficient to offset the Hormuz supply relief.
drivers: US-Iran preliminary agreement to halt hostilities and reopen the Strait of Hormuz triggered the day's sharp sell-off, removing a key geopolitical risk premium
Month-to-date losses of ~20% on WTI and Brent reflect a sustained supply-return narrative; CME options now price a 77% chance of an OPEC production cut at the next meeting

Offsetting geopolitical noise — UK interception of a Russian shadow-fleet tanker, new EU energy sanctions on Russia, and Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil infrastructure — failed to materially support prices
sources: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos

gas.summary: Henry Hub edged up 0.99% to $3.151/MMBtu, holding a solid +8.88% gain over the past month even as the broader energy complex sold off sharply. The US domestic market appears relatively insulated from the Hormuz deal that hammered oil, though European natural gas prices tumbled roughly 6% on the same news as LNG supply route risk eased. GasBuddy's petroleum analyst confirmed US national average retail gasoline has slipped below $4/gallon, a politically significant threshold. Goldman Sachs-backed Danish trader InCommodities is expanding into US physical gas markets after European trading profits collapsed as volatility faded — a signal that the European gas market is settling while US markets retain relative appeal. The data provided is somewhat limited for a full Henry Hub fundamental picture today.
drivers: Henry Hub diverged from the oil sell-off, edging higher on the day and sustaining a near 9% monthly gain, reflecting distinct US domestic supply-demand dynamics
European gas prices fell ~6% on the US-Iran Hormuz agreement, easing LNG supply-route risk premiums that had supported European prices
US retail gasoline slipping below $4/gallon reduces consumer inflation pressure but may dampen near-term refinery throughput and associated gas demand signals

power.summary: EU carbon allowances (EUA) bucked the broader energy sell-off, gaining 3.46% on the day to $75.575/EUA and posting a solid +6.65% monthly advance. The headline driver set for this sector is relatively thin today, but a handful of meaningful themes emerge. UK Prime Minister Starmer pledged new sanctions on Russia and nuclear energy support for Ukraine, while a separate UK energy deal was announced to support Ukrainian power infrastructure suffering from Russian attacks. India's federal government urged states to fast-track approvals for nuclear and battery storage projects. JP Morgan flagged that falling oil prices could prompt central bank rate cuts — a potential tailwind for capital-intensive clean energy investment. The divergence of EUA strength against weaker fossil fuel prices is consistent with a market repricing the longer-term energy transition.
drivers: EU carbon EUAs rose 3.46% against the grain of the broader energy sell-off, extending a monthly gain of 6.65% as lower fossil fuel prices may reinforce structural decarbonisation policy momentum
UK government pledged nuclear energy support for Ukraine and new Russia sanctions targeting energy revenues, reinforcing European energy security and clean-power investment themes
India's push to fast-track nuclear and battery storage approvals signals emerging-market policy acceleration toward low-carbon capacity, a medium-term demand signal for carbon markets
